topics: 🔄 The Convert's Firstborn — did sons born before conversion create a legal firstborn?
👨‍👩‍👧 Fruitful and Multiply — does a convert's pre-conversion fatherhood count?
🕎 The Levite's Daughter — five sela redemption exemption from a gentile father
⚖️ The Disqualified Priest's Son — must a ḥalal redeem himself?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Who Counts as a Firstborn?
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 47a–47b
overview.hebrewSource: הָיוּ לוֹ בָּנִים בְּגַיּוּתוֹ וְנִתְגַּיֵּיר — רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אוֹמֵר: אֵין לוֹ בְּכוֹר לַנַּחֲלָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with a dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish: if a man fathered sons as a gentile and then converted, does his first son born after conversion count as a firstborn for the double inheritance portion? The same disagreement resurfaces over whether fathering children before conversion already fulfilled 'be fruitful and multiply.' The Gemara then works through mishnayot about mixed lineage — a convert's or maidservant's child, a Levite's or priest's daughter impregnated by a gentile — asking whose status determines the son's obligations. The daf ends with a new mishna: which offspring is a firstborn for both inheritance and priestly redemption, and the special case of a child born by caesarean section.

slides.title: 🔄 Does a Pre-Conversion Son Block Firstborn Status?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish on the convert's later-born son

lines.speaker: R' Yochanan
lines.text: He has no firstborn for inheritance — he already had רֵאשִׁית אוֹנוֹ, 'the first of his strength,' before he converted.

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: He does have a firstborn — a convert who just converted is legally like a newborn child. His gentile-born sons don't count at all.

lines.speaker: R' Yochanan
lines.text: Consistently, I say he already fulfilled 'be fruitful and multiply' through those earlier sons — the verse just wants the world inhabited.

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: Consistently, I say he has not fulfilled it — as a new legal person, it is as though he never had children.

callout.label: Why state both disputes?
callout.text: Each case needed independent teaching: one might have conceded inheritance but not fruitfulness, or vice versa, so the Gemara spells out both.

slides.title: 🕎 Whose Womb, Whose Status?
slides.subtitle: Tracing the mishna's redemption exemptions to their source
rows: Levite's daughter, pregnant by a gentile
Rav Pappa: even those who 'disqualify' the child still follow the mother's tribe
Levite's daughter, pregnant by an Israelite
Disputed — Mar b. Rav Yosef says exempt
'Opening the womb' (פֶּטֶר רֶחֶם) hangs the law on the mother
Priest's daughter, pregnant by a gentile
If a gentile has relations with her she becomes like a non-priest — so why exempt her son?

callout.label: Rabba's resolution:
callout.text: A Levite woman retains her sanctity even after captivity or illicit relations and still eats tithe; a priest's daughter who has relations with a gentile loses her ability to eat teruma entirely — so the cases are not parallel.

slides.title: ⚖️ Must a Disqualified Priest's Son Redeem Himself?
slides.subtitle: Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna on a ḥalal whose father died young

nodes.content: ❓ A priest married a divorcée, had a son (a ḥalal), then died. Must the son redeem himself?
👨 Father died after 30 days: everyone agrees the son need not redeem himself — the father already 'acquired' the redemption as a priest

columns.label: Rav Ḥisda
columns.content: Father died within 30 days — son must redeem himself, since his father never acquired the money

columns.label: Rabba bar Rav Huna
columns.content: Son need not — he can say 'I stand in the shoes of a man you could never have sued'

nodes.content: 🌍 Challenge: a convert's son born pregnant does redeem himself, though his gentile father could never be sued — 'a gentile has no lineage' answers the difficulty

callout.label: Later ruling:
callout.text: Reish Lakish, cited by Rabbi Shimon Yasinia, sides with Rav Ḥisda: within 30 days the son must redeem himself; after 30 days he need not.

slides.title: 🍼 Mishna: Caesarean Birth and the Son Who Follows
slides.subtitle: Neither is a firstborn — but Rabbi Shimon splits the difference

boxes.title: The Caesarean Child
items: Not firstborn for inheritance — 'and they bore him children' requires a normal birth
Not firstborn for redemption — 'opens the womb' requires opening it

boxes.title: The Son Who Follows
items: Not firstborn for inheritance — not 'the first of his strength'
Not firstborn for redemption — a firstborn 'for one matter only' is not a firstborn at all, per the first tanna

boxes.title: Rabbi Shimon's View
items: The caesarean child IS firstborn for inheritance — 'she bears' (Lev. 12:5) includes caesarean birth
The son who follows IS firstborn for redemption — a firstborn 'for one matter' still counts

callout.label: Also in the mishna:
callout.text: A woman miscarrying a water-sac, blood-sac, fish-like or grasshopper-like mass, or one who miscarries by day 40, does not disqualify the next son from full firstborn status.

slides.title: 🔀 Establishing an Uncertain Firstborn's Claims
slides.subtitle: How the mishna's ruling on inheritance authorization gets explained

steps.content: 1️⃣ A woman who didn't wait three months, remarried, and gave birth — unclear if 9-month son of husband #1 or 7-month son of husband #2
2️⃣ Mishna: firstborn for priestly redemption, but not for inheritance — yet he still takes a share like an ordinary son
3️⃣ Rabbi Yirmeya: the ruling really targets the NEXT son (from husband #2) — he is not the firstborn, since this uncertain son might outrank him
4️⃣ Rabbi Yannai's principle: sons once individually recognized, later intermingled, may write authorization to each other to jointly claim the double portion

callout.label: Why authorization works here:
callout.text: Because each son was clearly identified before the confusion arose, each can act as the other's agent to claim what one of them certainly deserves.

summary.principle: Firstborn status for inheritance and for priestly redemption follow different verses and different logic — a child's status can depend on whether the mother's or father's lineage, or the manner of birth, satisfies each requirement.

flowSteps.content: 🔄 A convert's pre-conversion sons: do they block a later firstborn? R' Yochanan says yes, Reish Lakish says no
🕎 Levite/priest daughters impregnated by gentiles or Israelites — redemption exemption traced to 'opening the womb'

columns.content: ⚖️ Ḥalal priest's son redeems himself only if father died within 30 days
🍼 Caesarean birth: neither child is firstborn per the first tanna; R' Shimon splits the two halakhot

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: 'Bore him children' governs inheritance; 'opens the womb' governs redemption — and they need not point to the same child

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, does a man who had sons as a gentile and then converted have a firstborn for inheritance purposes among sons born after conversion?
o: Yes, the first son born after conversion always inherits a double portion
No — he already had 'the first of his strength' before converting
Only if he had no daughters
Only if his gentile-born sons had died
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that the pre-conversion son already satisfied 'the first of his strength,' so no later son can be a firstborn for inheritance.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rav Pappa, is the son of a Levite's daughter who became pregnant from a gentile exempt from the five-sela redemption?
o: Because gentiles are never obligated in mitzvot
Because the mother retains her Levite sanctity even after such relations, unlike a priest's daughter
Because the son is considered a firstborn only for inheritance
Because gentiles cannot father firstborn sons at all
quiz.e: Rabba explains that a Levite woman retains her sanctity (she can still eat tithe) even after captivity or illicit relations, so her son follows her Levite status; a priest's daughter loses her priestly eating rights in the same situation.

quiz.q: Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna disagree about a ḥalal (disqualified priest's) son whose priest-father died. When do they disagree?
o: Whenever the father dies
Only if the father died after 30 days from the son's birth
Only if the father died within 30 days from the son's birth
They never disagree
quiz.e: Everyone agrees that if the father died after 30 days, he already 'acquired' the redemption money as a priest, so the son need not redeem himself. They disagree only about death within 30 days.

quiz.q: According to the first tanna of the mishna, is a child born by caesarean section a firstborn for inheritance or redemption?
o: Firstborn for both
Firstborn for inheritance only
Firstborn for redemption only
Firstborn for neither
quiz.e: The first tanna holds the caesarean child is firstborn for neither: inheritance requires 'and they bore him children' (a normal birth), and redemption requires 'opening the womb.'

quiz.q: Per Rabbi Yannai's principle cited by Rabbi Yirmeya, when can two sons whose identities became confused write authorization to each other to jointly claim a double portion?
o: Only if neither was ever individually recognized
Only if each was individually recognized before becoming intermingled
Never — authorization is invalid for inheritance claims
Only if they are twins
quiz.e: Rabbi Yannai teaches that authorization works only when the sons were initially recognized and later became mixed up; if neither was ever recognized, authorization is ineffective since neither had a clear prior claim.
